client: Lately, I've been feeling completely drained trying to juggle my nursing shifts and taking care of my kids while my partner is away. I feel like I'm constantly dropping the ball somewhere, either at work or at home, and it's making me really anxious. I'm not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like there's just not enough hours in the day to get everything done.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying an overwhelming load right now, and that constant pressure is leaving you feeling stretched thin and anxious. When you think about "dropping the ball," what specific thoughts go through your mind about what that means?

client: I keep imagining my supervisor thinking I'm incompetent when I forget small details at work, and then at home I worry my kids will resent me for always being tired. Today I forgot to pack my daughter's lunch and had to leave work early to bring it to school - I feel like I'm failing everyone. But honestly, even if I identify these thoughts, what difference does it make? The problems are still there.
therapist: The weight of these thoughts—about being seen as incompetent or resented—sounds like it’s adding even more exhaustion to an already overwhelming situation. When you notice these thoughts, do you ever find moments where the evidence might not fully support them, like times you’ve handled things well despite the stress?

client: I guess there was that one day last week when I managed to get all my charting done on time and still made it to my son's soccer game. But that feels like the exception, not the rule. It's hard to focus on those small wins when most days I'm barely keeping my head above water.
therapist: It sounds like you’re dismissing that small win because it feels overshadowed by the harder days, which makes sense when you’re under so much pressure. What would it feel like to pause for a moment and really acknowledge that success—even if it’s just one day—as proof that you’re capable, even in this tough situation?

client: I don't know... focusing on that one good day almost makes the rest feel worse by comparison. Like "see, you can do it sometimes, so why can't you do it all the time?" That just makes me feel more guilty. Aren't I supposed to be able to handle this? Other nurses with kids seem to manage.
therapist: It sounds like focusing on that one good day is bringing up feelings of guilt and self-doubt, especially when you compare yourself to others. What if we shifted the focus slightly—instead of asking “why can’t I do it all the time,” could we explore what made that one day different and whether any of those factors could help on the harder days?

client: Well... that day I actually got a full night's sleep because my neighbor took the kids for an evening. But I can't ask her to do that all the time - she has her own life. And meal prep helped too, but who has time for that regularly? I see what you're getting at, but it feels like these solutions aren't sustainable.
therapist: It sounds like you’re noticing some helpful strategies—like support from your neighbor and meal prep—but it’s hard to see how they can fit into your regular routine. When you think about sustainability, what smaller, more manageable steps might make a difference, even if they don’t solve everything right away?

client: I guess I could try prepping just one meal for the week instead of trying to do everything at once. But even that feels like just one more thing to add to my plate. And honestly, I feel guilty asking for help—like I should be able to handle this on my own. Isn’t that what everyone expects of me?
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting to make things easier for yourself and feeling like you "should" be able to handle everything alone. That guilt and pressure to meet expectations must be really heavy. What would it feel like to challenge that idea—that asking for help or taking small steps means you're not capable enough?

client: It’s hard to challenge that idea because it feels like admitting weakness. Like if I ask for help, I’m proving to everyone—and myself—that I can’t do it all. Plus, I worry people will judge me or think I’m not cut out for this. But I also know I can’t keep going like this forever—it’s exhausting. I just don’t know how to balance it all without feeling like I’m failing.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of fear tied to asking for help—like it would confirm something negative about your abilities. But when you say it’s exhausting and can’t go on forever, it seems like you’re recognizing that trying to do it all alone might not be sustainable. What would it feel like to reframe asking for help as a strength—a way to take care of yourself so you can keep doing the things that matter most?

client: I never thought of it that way—as a strength rather than weakness. But it's still hard. At work, we're always told to be self-sufficient, and at home I'm supposed to be the rock for my kids. The idea of showing vulnerability in either place makes me feel exposed. What if people start viewing me differently because I can't just power through like they expect?
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot at stake for you in showing vulnerability—whether it’s at work or at home—and that fear of being seen differently is really holding you back. What would it mean to you if, instead of being judged, others responded with understanding or even admiration for your honesty?

client: I guess part of me would feel relieved if people responded that way, but it's hard to imagine. The nurses I work with all seem to have it together, and I don't want to be the one who can't keep up. But... I did see a coworker struggling last month and I actually respected her more when she asked for help instead of making mistakes. Maybe I'm holding myself to a different standard?
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to notice that asking for help doesn’t diminish someone’s abilities—it actually shows strength and self-awareness. But it’s interesting that while you respected your coworker for doing it, it’s harder to offer yourself the same kindness. What do you think might be different about the standard you hold for yourself compared to others?

client: I think I hold myself to an impossible standard because deep down, I'm terrified of being seen as replaceable - at work or at home. But that's exhausting, and now that you point it out, it does feel unfair that I wouldn't judge a coworker the way I judge myself. Still, old habits are hard to break.
therapist: It sounds like you're recognizing how much this fear of being replaceable has driven you—and how exhausting that standard is to maintain. That unfair double standard (judging yourself harshly while offering grace to others) is something many people struggle to change. What would it feel like to try small experiments—like intentionally asking for help with one small thing—to test whether the feared outcomes actually happen?
